speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am afraid this is abusing the House. The Hon. Member is really making a mockery of our rules. It is for the sake of decorum and for the protection of the House that we have certain rules. I do not see how the Hon. Member can think he can get out of that.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I would remind the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) that the Member for Gatineau (Mrs. Mailly) is right in her point of order. I give the floor to the Member for Yorkton-Melville.

I suppose that comes from her vast experience. Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker.
We had a conference in Quebec and a lot of talk about free trade, improved relations between Americans and Canadians, and how this would be of great benefit for Canada. Yet, as soon as the President left, there was the announcement of a 12 per cent tariff on Canadian hogs. The Canadian hog industry is worth around $2 billion per year to the Canadian economy. Only a few days ago there was an announcement that States such as Iowa, Nebraska and Oklahoma were banning the importation of Canadian hogs. Where is this new relationship, Mr. Speaker? What does free trade mean for this country? Is it free trade for Canada but protectionism for the United States?
It is due to such actions as I described that farmers of the country need more protection and more money. For that reason I recommend that the House introduce legislation to provide farmers with a guarantee on cost of production and a decent return. I was very pleased that the House referred to committee the subject matter of Bill C-235 on parity pricing. That Bill would provide farmers with their costs of production and a decent return. It would cover wheat, oats, barley, hogs, and beef. For the portion consumed in this country the farmer would receive a parity price based on the cost of production. I do not think that is asking too much. It is asking for no more than what other Canadians receive for the work they do. As Members of Parliament we are often criticized for our high salaries. Perhaps the Canadian population is right that we are overpaid for what we produce. Obviously, that was the opinion last summer because over half the Members did not come back. However, MPs' salaries are adjusted every year according to the cost of living, as is the case with other people in our
society who have collective agreements. Even senior citizens get a minuscule increase of $3 or $4 every three months on their pension cheques if the cost of living goes up.
The argument made by our Party and by an increasing number of farmers in Canada is that they too should be paid a price that has some relevance to what it costs them to produce a bushel of wheat or raise a hog on the farm, a price that has some relevance to the cost of repairs on their tractors or to the interest rate or price of fuel in this country.
That is what farmers are telling this Parliament. The concept of parity pricing means that farmers do not want a subsidy, a hand-out or a charity. All they want is a fair price from the market-place so that if interest rates, fuel or the price of machinery go up, the price that a Canadian pays for a loaf of bread or a bottle of beer will go up as well. I do not think that is asking for too much. Let us use wheat as an example. If the price of wheat goes up $5 a bushel and the farmer were to receive the entire $5 a bushel for the increase in the price of wheat, the price of a loaf of bread for the Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) would go up eight cents a loaf. I ask: is an extra eight cents a loaf too much to pay to give the farmer an extra $5 a bushel for the wheat he is producing to make that bread? Perhaps the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) indulges from time to time and wants to have a beer.
I don't drink.

Let us say the Member from Newfoundland wanted a beer. If we raised the price of beer by 40 cents a dozen and gave all of that 40 cents to the farmer who produces malting barley for the beer, the price of malting barley would go up $10 a bushel.
We can afford that in this country. If we had a price based on the cost of production and on a decent return, we could keep many more farmers on the land, solve many farm bankruptcy problems in this country, and provide more jobs to young people from coast to coast since farming is the base industry in this country.
There are other examples besides bread and beer. The corn farmers of Ontario will know that often it costs more to run contests for cereals with respect to processing the coupons and advertising the contents than what the farmer gets for the corn that goes into the cornflakes.
I have never heard of anyone winning, anyway.

The Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) says that he has never heard of anyone who won. Maybe it is because he is in the wrong Party. I think there is something terribly wrong in our society if the farmer receives less than what it costs to process a coupon on a cereal box.
We believe that the farmer should get a parity price that is based on the cost of production. It would stimulate the small
May 17, 1985

business community and provide more jobs for young people. It would stimulate the entire Canadian economy.
This can be done without a subsidy. It can be done without increasing the national debt. It can be done without imposing more taxes on the Canadian people. I believe that it is the kind of direction we should be taking in our society today.
The Government often speaks of the huge Liberal debt with which it was saddled. I repeat that the farmers are not asking for a hand-out, but for a more fair share of the proceeds from the market-place. I believe we can afford to pay that in this country.

I think the crisis in agriculture is now very serious in this country. I have here a list of farm bankruptcies over the last 6 or 7 years in this country.
Six years ago, in 1979, there were 125 farm bankruptcies in Canada. The following year, 1980, 220 farms went bankrupt. In 1981, there were 261; in 1982, 410; in 1983, 488; in 1984, more than 500, yes 551 farmers went bankrupt here in Canada. And during the first quarter of 1985, 152 farmers went bankrupt across Canada. This is a very serious situation. It is very serious in Quebec, very serious in my own Province of Saskatchewan, very serious across the entire country.
Mr. Speaker, six years ago, in 1979, farm indebtedness in Canada was $14.6 billion. Two years later, it had increased to $18.5 billion. And, last year, in 1984, farm indebtedness In Canada totalled $20.7 billion.

We have had an increase in the farm debt from 1979 to 1984 from $14.6 billion to $20.7 billion. Farm incomes have not gone up. The realized net income of farmers in 1975, was some $3.8 billion. In 1978, it was $3.1 billion. In 1981, it was $4.2 billion. In 1983, it was $3.3 billion and in 1984, it was $3.8 billion. The realized net income of farmers in 1984 was exactly what it was in 1975, that is, $3.8 billion. Although nine years have passed, farmers' income has not gone up. I suggest that something is terribly wrong in our system.
I suggest that Bill C-25 is no different from the Bill introduced in the last Parliament by the Liberals and Mr. Whelan as Minister of Agriculture. Perhaps that is why my hon. friend from the Liberal Party was so anxious to jump into bed with the Conservative Government earlier this morning and again this afternoon in promising support at second reading for this particular Bill. It is the same type of Bill that we have seen before.
I suggest that this Bill is inadequate because it stabilizes farm incomes at 90 per cent of the previous Five-year average. Would Members of Parliament agree to pass a Bill in the House that would stabilize our incomes as MPs at 90 per cent of our previous five-year average? That would be a disaster for the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Beatty) because he would lose half of his taxes. Yet we are being asked to pass legislation that would have that effect on farmers.
Agricultural Stabilization Act
A second major concern is one which will anger Quebec farmers. Some provinces have provincial income insurance programs. In Quebec, it is based on the cost of production of hog farmers and others. The same situation exists in British Columbia. Farmers in those provinces will not qualify for this federal stabilization program. I do not believe that it is fair that a province and its farmers should be penalized by a federal program because that province is enlightened and progressive with respect to an income insurance program. I appeal to my friends to make that change in the committee so that we would not penalize the farmers of Quebec and British Columbia.
I remind the House that according to the Constitution of Canada, agriculture is co-jurisdictional. It comes under the responsibility of both the federal Government and the provinces. Both the provinces and the federal Parliament have the right to legislate, and the provinces should not be penalized by federal legislation, as is the case with this federal legislation. I appeal again to my colleagues to make that particular change. Most important, we need legislation that will give the farmer his cost of production back and a decent return. I think we have a consensus today. We have a consensus for parity prices in western Canada, in Quebec, and in parts of Ontario, and I appeal to this House to get on with it and to provide the farmers with legislation that will help each and every one of them.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak on Bill C-25, an Act to amend the Agricultural Stabilization Act. There is a critical need to reshape this part of the agricultural industry in Canada.
I have listened to my hon. colleagues across the floor. I heard the cute rat, the mean rat, the shrill rat and the Newfie rat talk about the slowness of this Government to introduce legislation. Yet I remember the time last week when a Member on the other side stood up and said: "I have spoken four times on this Bill this week". Anyone on the other side who is trying to blame this Government for delaying tactics on this Bill is simply not telling the truth.
I have heard a socialist Member talk about guaranteeing income. He would have every farmer on the government payroll. Farmers would have no incentive for free enterprise, for making money and getting ahead. This is totally unacceptable based on our deficit position. It would be unacceptable in any case because it would run us into a deficit.
I represent the riding of Perth in southwestern Ontario. Within my riding is the City of Stratford, and within that city is the flagship of Canadian theatre. We have a diversified riding. Next week the Stratford Shakespearian Festival will open its thirty-third season. It is quite a coincidence in that we are now in our thirty-third Parliament. Surrounding the City of Stratford is the beautiful County of Perth. I have some of the best farmers farming some of the best farm land in Canada. I know that is also true of the county south of me and around me, the County of Oxford.

May 17, 1985
Agricultural Stabilization Act
These days, however, many farmers are hurting. The stage was set a few years ago when Canada was caught in an inflation spiral that was pushed along by our Liberal predecessors. At the time, the psychology was that if you did not invest, inflation would kill you, but if you did invest, inflation was supposed to pull you out. Later, spiralling interest rates and low commodity prices brought Canada to the ground. Now the survivors as well are hurting from unfair competition both from outside and from inside Canada. The outside competition is most obvious. It comes from the European Economic Community. That community has a policy of self-sufficiency in food. The EEC has subsidized products without care for the amount produced.
We were hit when the EEC changed its policy. Instead of producing 150 per cent of the needs of the EEC, 125 per cent of its meat and dairy requirements were produced. This brought the EEC to the point where one-sixth of its dairy herd cattle was slaughtered, resulting in mountains of boned frozen meat, which created our problem. There was so much meat, the EEC had to rent facilities outside of the community for storage purposes. When one has high storage costs, it is not too hard to realize that the next step is subsdization of sales. Meat arrived at Canada's border with an export subsidy of 35 per cent. This was less than the original subsidy after appeals from the Government.
Last year, Canada's farmers had to compete with 50 million pounds of beef from the EEC that was subsidized well over 35 per cent, probably in the range of 60 per cent. Figures show that European farmers get about 39 per cent of their income from Governments while Canadian farmers get only 12 per cent.
I know that our Ontario farmers would not want to have subsidies. They can and will compete with farmers the world over, but they cannot compete with foreign treasuries, for instance, the EEC. One must hope that the EEC will come to its senses soon and decrease subsidies. But even then, Mr. Speaker, we will still be faced with the impact of the subsidies as we have in the dairy cut-backs.
Outside competition also exists in Canada. Farmers in one area compete with provincial treasuries in other provinces. This is why Bill C-25 is so important because it will open a path to a uniform subsidy plan across Canada.
Some regions of Canada are more suited to certain forms of agriculture than are others. I believe all will accept that western Canada is particularly suited to beef production because of its thousands of acres of grassland. As well, southwestern Ontario is blessed with good land and a favourable climate. Perhaps even more important, southwestern Ontario is close to the major population centres of Ontario and our export market. Other areas of Canada do not have the same advantage and agriculture there does not flourish as well.
However, few provincial Governments can accept that. Agriculture, when it is thriving, can make the rest of the country go. It is one of the most potent, perhaps the most potent, economic forces that exist. Therefore, provinces have established their own forms of subsidy. Even to speak about
these subsidies is most difficult. Until very recently there was no compilation of support policies across Canada. There is now a report in this connection in the draft stage.
If we speak about swine, Mr. Speaker, perhaps the best source of information would be the U.S.A. where interest groups have studied our program to defend the imposition of countervailing duties.
We can accept in general that farmers in the EEC get 39 per cent of their income through their Governments, in the U.S.A. about 36 per cent, while Canadian farmers get only about 12 per cent. The support in Canada is not equal. It is an average of all the support. Ontario and Alberta, the have provinces which contribute to the equalization payments that help other provincial treasuries, have the lowest subsidies. Perhaps because of the natural advantages on which I have already touched, these farmers survive. These farmers are now competing with farmers who are more heavily subsidized in other provinces, subsidized perhaps with money sent in equalization payments.
Examples of provincial subsidies can best be shown in the hog industry. I would like to speak of the hog industry because Perth County produces more hogs than any other similar area in Canada.
In Prince Edward Island the subsidy can best be described as bipartite or coming from two parties, the provincial Government and the producer. The enrolled producers are supported to a level of 95 per cent of the total operational costs of an efficient producer. These costs include depreciation and interest charges. If the price of hogs goes up, the farmers begin to donate to the stabilization fund.
If one accepts that the costs in eastern Canada are higher and prices are set according to Ontario and to export prices, it is easy to see that this fund will nearly always be in a deficit position with the money coming continually from the provincial treasury. In 1984, this program cost Prince Edward Island nearly $1 million.
In Quebec, enrolled farmers have income stabilized to include their cost plus 70 per cent to 100 per cent of a specialized workers' income. Farmers do participate in this plan but the Government input is always twice that of the hog producer. I understand that in 1984, enrolled Quebec farmers received approximately $24 a hog. If the provincial treasury paid its two-thirds share, then each hog was subsidized to the tune of $16. Of course, all of these programs are based on good average producers. Farmers with better graded hogs, and the more efficient ones, received the subsidy and a profit.
If we get back to Ontario and Alberta farmers, we find only the subsidies that farmers get across Canada, for example, some relief in taxes, some assistance with drainage, and some interest relief for beginning farmers or farmers in difficulty. The Ontario hog farmer does get a stabilization payment under the Agricultural Stabilization Act if prices are low compared to a five-year average. This takes the bumps out of the rapidly changing hog prices, but it does not guarantee a profit. We are aiming to keep the farmers on the farm in times
May 17, 1985

of drastic cuts rather than to keep them on the farm with a guaranteed profit. In 1984, a payment was made. In 1985, there will be no payment. Not only do Ontario farmers have no subsidy this year, but they must compete with farmers whose hogs are subsidized. The Ontario production of hogs is about equal to the consumption in Ontario. However, other provinces sell thousands of live hogs in our market. Other countries, like Denmark, also penetrate our market. Then our surplus hogs find their way to the American market.
When we speak of the American market we must mention countervailing duties. The strong American dollar and government policies are combining to put unusual pressure on the American farmer. With an increasing amount of our pork entering the American market-and it is only a fraction of that market-American farmers thought it was unnecessary and unfair and successfully moved to have a countervailing duty applied. This duty was defended on the basis of a Canadian subsidy. Ironically it is the Ontario farmer who bears the brunt of this duty, while it is other parts of the country, particularly those to the east, which obtain the subsidy or are cushioned from the effect of subsidy by income guarantees.
We have heard comment about our friendship with the American Government and with the American President. In June the President of the United States will have to decide whether the duties will be applied. He has the final signing authority. The process up until now did not involve a presidential decision. I submit to the House that it is fine for us to have a good relationship with the President of the United States rather than the controversial relationship of the past. If there is a chance for this duty to be removed, there is more of a chance now than there was at any other time.
I hope I have laid the groundwork to demonstrate that a national tripartite scheme is essential. It should not be thought that every region in Canada should be subsidized in relation to its particular costs. Pork produced in Canada is Canadian pork, and all producers should produce on an equal basis. This is particularly important when one considers that present plans encourage over-production and that our subsidized products are exported to foreign buyers. Such a common system will become possible with the amendments proposed under Bill C-25. Four provinces have already agreed that tripartite plans should be in place-Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta-which represent somewhat over half the producers in Canada. They only await legislation for the plan to go ahead. To delay passage of this Bill any longer would place pressure on these provinces to initiate their own plans and to enter the interprovincial wars of treasuries being fought in farmers' backyards.
Under a tripartite agreement, the provinces would drop their regional subsidies and production in Canada would fall back to a more rational, market sensitive level. Each participant-the provinces, the federal Government and enrolled producers- would pay equal shares. Unlike present provincial plans, the
Agricultural Stabilization Act
maximum amount of any government input would be 3 per cent of gross sales of the product. In certain circumstances I understand the producer might be allowed to increase his payments to obtain a bigger pay-out.
The tripartite agreement would allow payments to be made promptly in respect of those products lending themselves to quarterly adjustments. For instance, for hogs and feeder cattle payments could be made on a quarterly basis. For other crops like wheat, payments could be made at the end of a crop season. The tripartite support prices would be such that there would be no incentive to over-produce and each commodity would have its own fund, recognizing the unique characteristics of the commodity, for instance, the difference in a cow-calf operation where costs are relatively static and the calf comes once a year, and the production of backgrounders, a term I never heard until I came to Ottawa, which means light feeder cattle, where the turnover can be as little as three months.
Within the tripartite agreements will be provisions that pay-outs will occur only on domestically consumed products. The Americans have shown more understanding of similar plans, and under such plans countervailing duties would be less likely.
Certainly the farmers of Ontario will welcome this Bill with its great potential to bring stability to farm incomes. Other farmers, particularly those who are benefiting from generous schemes, schemes funded partially by equilization payments from the have provinces, will initially fear the effects. However, our farmers are important to the nation and agriculture is an important tool to our economy. We cannot allow provincial boundaries to become the battle lines between farmers. We cannot afford to pour in more money, funded by loans, to push production in less favoured areas while the more favoured, efficient areas are torn down. The agreements which are possible under the amendments to the Agricultural Stabilization Act are important to the future of Canadian farmers. I am pleased to be able to add my support to its passage.

Mr. Speaker, I want to correct an impression which I think the Hon. Member did not intend to leave. This is not a stabilization of farm income Bill; it is a stabilization of commodity prices Bill. One of its weaknesses is that it attempts to stabilize the commodity price. If the market price continues to go down, the result will be a lower stabilized price every year.
Following upon his remarks, I would like to ask the Hon. Member a question. He abhors the import of subsidized products into the country. I suppose that is a real concern on the part of all of us who are either farmers or deal with farmers or with products that have to compete with these imports. In the case of EEC beef, would the Hon. Member explain why his Government did not do something else rather than cave in to the EEC and increase the quota? Originally it was 5.9 per cent, and now we understand that the level will be three times that amount. Why did the Government do that? It invites more beef into the country to compete with Canadian beef.

May 17, 1985
Agricultural Stabilization Act

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his question. The problem with European beef started, as I mentioned in my speech, when the EEC suddenly had surplus beef which it had to dispose of and subsidized its sale. Canadian beef farmers became aware of the problem and tried to set up a hearing under the GATT agreement to see if it could be withdrawn. We understand that last August a decision was made within the bureaucracy indicating that frozen boned beef was not in fact a beef product, that beef producers could not appeal, and that if there was to be an appeal it would have to be done by the producers of frozen meat products. That occurred last August before this Government was involved. As the problem grew, the Government applied a restriction and held hearings. The amount of meat coming into Canada has been drastically reduced. I have not heard the final decision, but it would seem that we have either to accept that amount of meat, because the problems were created before we came into power, or to pay the penalty of $50 million. It should be remembered that the quota about which we are talking is less than half the amount of beef which came in last year. It is probably less than a third of the amount of meat which would have come in this year if we had not taken the strong action we took.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is forgetting the other side of the problem, that is, the threat to other industries. Because of the quota which has been established and the failure to take action to make it less profitable for this beef to come into the country by establishing a countervailing duty, or something of that nature, we are threatening other products such as honey and maple syrup. In fact, I could provide a list of some 20 products. What fear does the Government have about placing a countervailing duty on this beef? Everyone accepts the idea that it is subsidized. The last figure I heard was probably as high as $1 per kilogram. That would mean that we would put a fairly hefty tariff on it within the GATT.

Mr. Speaker, I was fully aware of the penalties that were being threatened by the European Economic Community. I was there in March. We were told that Canada had two choices, either to negotiate on the basis of accepting more meat and paying the penalties on products coming in, or go for an agreement under the GATT. That is still open to us. To go under the GATT takes time. The product floods in in even greater amounts. This is probably a self-limiting amount. When the surplus is exhausted, we will not be flooded with beef from the European Economic Community. It will probably come from some other area, and we will have to watch that.
We were put in the position that we had to negotiate. If we apply more duties on this, we involve a large group with far greater power and more trading aspects. We are in surplus trade with them and they can penalize us even more. We cannot do it without a negotiated settlement, what we are approaching right now.

The United States did not wait. They did not have to go through the GATT process, which takes a long time. I agree that it does. The United States put on a countervailing duty against our hogs which went into effect immediately. The money is going into a trust. It has had the effect of reducing the price of pork from 75 cents in some areas, and even to 58 cents the other day. If the United States can do that under GATT, why can Canada not do the same on beef?

Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a few comments. First, we are dealing with the United States which is dealing with another group of equal power. Second, the hearings in the United States did not occur immediately. The Hon. Member simply is not informed. They went through at least three stages. At the present time, they are still not complete. These duties that are being collected could come back, subject to the decision which will be handed down June 7. It was not an immediate decision. I do not know under what law it was done, but it was probably under the GATT. I could be informed about that. I do not know how it was done.

Yes, Mr. Speaker, it could possibly be returned. The effect of that return will not help the farmer who sold the pork unless he sold it through a marketing board, in only a couple of provinces. It has had the effect of making it unprofitable to ship our pork to the United States, consequently reducing the effective income of the hog farmer.

Mr. Speaker, I acknowledge that the countervailing duties have had the effect of reducing prices, probably from 73 cents to 63 cents. There is a philosophy that may be having an effect on the total North American market. At the same time as our prices are coming down, American prices have come down as well. Our dollar has fluctuated to a degree. Therefore, there have been other factors than the countervailing duties.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Resuming debate.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to make a few comments on Bill C-25, an Act to provide some stabilization to red meat prices in this country.
I should begin by stating that I have never had a great deal of expertise, in fact I have very little, with respect to agriculture in this country. In my part of the country the fishery and forestry are the resource industries and primary areas for job creation. There are a number of small farmers in my riding. I have taken an interest and tried to learn something about the difficulty that farmers encounter. Earlier this week I had the opportunity to meet with some gentlemen from the great Province of Alberta, members of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. They came to my office to begin the process of educating me. They told me of the difficulties that farmers in this country face in trying to make a living, trying to provide food for our tables in Canada and elselwhere around the world. At the same time, they are trying to make a decent living for themselves and their families.
May 17, 1985

I rise today to support Bill C-25. There is no question that the Bill is necessary. Although there is a fair amount of controversy within the agricultural community about whether it represents a solid step in the right direction vis-a-vis the American threats of countervail and the American attitude with respect to fish and lumber, and in recent days we saw prevention of the importation of pork into their country, nevertheless until somebody comes up with a better solution I feel I have no choice but to support the notion of a tripartite red meat stabilization program.
Marketing stability has been a common characteristic of beef and pork producers. Even though prices over the years, particularly on the red meat side since 1974, have been very unstable, fluctuating up and down, these producers nevertheless have the responsibility to make long-term investment decisions. Those decisions carry with them a responsibility to undertake long-term repayment programs. It is very difficult when you do not know from year to year what kind of return you will have on your investment. It is difficult to know whether you can provide a reasonable return on your investment and a reasonable income for your family in the first instance. In the final analysis, and more important, you do not know whether you will have the kind of income to meet those long-term mortgage payments. If Bill C-25 prevents to some degree the fluctuation in market prices and ensures that producers can make long-term plans and at least have some assurance of a base price for their product, I support the Bill.
I have one problem with the Bill coming up at this time. We have seen reports in recent days, such as the one I have before me in which the general manager of the Saskatchewan Pork Producers Marketing Board, Mr. Jim Morris, has indicated that the farm commodity stabilization programs, the whole range of those programs across Canada, may have to be dismantled if producers want to continue selling in the U.S. market without paying heavy penalties.
When you have someone of that calibre and that kind of interest and input in this industry coming back from the United States, talking to producers in that country, suggesting that on the countervail side Canada may be in serious difficulty unless we begin to dismantle stabilization programs, and we may see more and more protectionist measures being adopted in that country to prevent the import of Canadian products, then I am a bit concerned that perhaps we have to do our homework before this Bill is passed. We ought to be sure that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) have received assurances from our friends to the south that the net result of passing Bill C-25 will not be a knee-jerk reaction south of the border. Every one in this House is familiar with the news reports of the last few days of western produced pork being prohibited from going south of the border. I am a bit concerned about that kind of trend spreading to red meat if we pass this Bill without first assuring ourselves of the reaction it will receive south of the border.
Agricultural Stabilization Act
I repeat that I support the Bill. The Bill does not solve all the problems of the agricultural community in this country. It is a very small step, a temporary solution, taken before these trade discussions with our neighbours to the south have been concluded. As one who is not familiar with farming, one who did not grow up in a farming environment and does not understand the blood, sweat and tears, the part of your life that a farmer invests in trying to make a living from the land, I received a message. I did not entirely appreciate it. For the first time, a few days ago, I had a good discussion with some farmers. I was given a look at the way farmers' incomes have moved over the last 10 years. I saw that even though cash flow associated with the farming operation has increased dramatically, even though the cost of equipment and competitive technology has increased dramatically, and even though the number of bankruptcies are on the rise, real farm income over the last 10 or 12 years has not moved.
It seems to me that parliamentarians have the responsibility to ensure that there is a degree of justice and fairness for people who have chosen to make their living on farms. Through my discussions I learned that farmers have not had any real or significant increases in their incomes over the last 10 years. If there were any other single group in society that could organize itself with one voice and had not had a real increase in income in the last 10 years it would be here on Parliament Hill demanding that the Government pay serious attention to its problems.
The solution is not simple. Obviously one of the most important problems with which we as parliamentarians must come to grips is in providing farmers and those in the agricultural community with the ability to borrow money at interest rates that allow them to make a decent living and retain some cash at the end of the year that can be reinvested in their farms to keep their farms productive and to keep the Canadian agricultural industry competitive.
The Government made a great many promises to farmers during last summer's election. As one who knows very little about this industry, but is going to learn more, I will assume that those promises were made in good faith. If those promises were made in good faith, and if pledges to assist farmers and allow them to live with dignity and a sense of just reward meant anything at all, then the Government had better come forward with a program that will allow farmers to borrow money from FCC or on the open market at interest rates that reflect their ability to repay. As it stands right now, we are driving farmers into the ground.
One can only assume, looking at the data, that it must be a love of labour that keeps many of these people going. It certainly cannot be the financial reward involved. When looking at the kind of incomes farmers have, given their investment and their time spent sometimes over generations, they are not farming out of love of money.
I rise today to support the Bill before us. I would like to add that the farmers of Atlantic Canada are having a difficult time as well. When one hears red meat producers from Ontario,

May 17, 1985
Agricultural Stabilization Act
Quebec and elsewhere screaming that it is tough out there, one can be assured that it is twice as tough in Atlantic Canada, because the farmers of Atlantic Canada import feed and grain from Central Canada for their livestock. The producers of Atlantic Canada spend as much as 30 per cent to 35 per cent of their over-all costs bringing grain into the Atlantic region. Right now, the subsidies that have been paid over the years to bring that grain into Atlantic Canada are being eroded. We are seeing the Government move to increase freight rates through those Crown corporations which are responsible for moving freight in Atlantic Canada.
For the Atlantic Provinces, and particularly the island provinces of Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland, whenever there is an over-all increase in freight rates, the cost of living and the cost of doing business is affected. Moving things by freight to Newfoundland is not a question of taking the scenic route by the sea versus some other route. When there is bulk material that needs to be moved over 90 miles of water, the sea is the only way to go.
When dramatic increases are applied with no thought to the effect of those increases, the net result is a dramatic increase in the cost of living. In fact, when unemployment rates in most provinces went down three-tenths of 1 per cent, it went up 2.3 per cent in Newfoundland, due in large measure to the Government's move to increase freight rates to an island province where no other alternative is available for moving grain, livestock or consumable goods. The Government brought in an increase with no thought to its impact on the people of that province.
With those few words and with a great deal of humility, as a man who has much to learn-has barely scratched the surface-but has a passion for the difficulties of farmers, I urge Hon. Members to see this Bill passed in reasonable time.

Mr. Speaker, I have a comment to make to which the Hon. Member might like to add. I would point out to the Hon. Member that his knowledge of the primary industry of fishing gives him the kind of knowledge and authority required to speak on the problems of farmers. Their problems are very similar and have the same effect.
I appreciated particularly the Hon. Member's last words regarding transportation. The farmers and other producers in remote areas are affected by transportation costs. For example, I feel that Saskatchewan and other areas like the Peace River country are remote areas. By setting up increases in freight rates on a percentage basis, when those in the remote areas are already paying more than those who are closer to central Canada, a real penalty is put on those who live farther away from the market. That penalty then becomes a part of the cost of production to the farmer and the fisherman. If a farmer has to pay an extra dollar a bushel to ship his grain, that means he receives a dollar a bushel less. If the price of grain is set at $7 at Thunder Bay, the farmer in the Peace River country receives only $5. I appreciated the approach taken by the Hon. Member because it had not been taken previously.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his generosity. I was terrified that he was going to ask me some complex questions about a subject about which I admit freely I do not have a great deal of expertise.
Indeed, one of the approaches that is being taken by the Government that concerns me is its approach to the agricultural community. This approach affects the notion that people have the ability to choose where they want to live, and to have a life-style that is uniquely their own in the case of those who have lived in rural areas for hundreds of years. If these people are not actively supported, then at least they ought not to have difficulties placed in their way for choosing to live a certain life-style.
In the past, we always had the notion of regional development and regional assistance. As a goal, we wanted to remove regional disparities. We were trying to provide, at the very minimum, services to meet the basic needs and requirements of the people across this land on an equal basis.
I believe the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) has a somewhat different attitude. It is an attitude which indicates, "User-pay. That is the concept we shall apply." It is an attitude which indicates that those who live in the areas of the largest population shall benefit first and foremost from the services of the Government. I don't object to that, I really don't. But I believe that those who live in the rural areas, off the beaten path, and who have lived there for generations, choosing a life-style which reflects rural Canada, or the north, should also be able to expect the benefit of services and programs of the Government of Canada. But that is not the attitude taken by this Government which is too much concerned with a free market, private sector approach to providing goods and services to Canadians.
I am a free enterpriser from the word go. If I wanted to sell "rat pack" T-shirts, I would go out to the biggest marketplace, because that would make sense. I wouldn't go to a place where there are the least number of people. But the Government is elected to represent all of the people no matter where they live in this country. It has an obligation to understand and to empathize with all of the people no matter where they live or what their circumstances might be. The Government's kind of market-place mentality will lead us to the point where we will have first, second, third and fourth class citizenships. That is a step in the wrong direction, Mr. Speaker.
My colleague talked about farmers who live off the beaten path, who do not live on the main transportation routes, whose business is not adjacent to the major market areas, and the additional cost they must bear to produce and get their product to market. He has concern about the cost of transportation and this Government's approach to it. I suspect that we understand each other very well.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today to speak on Bill C-25, an Act to amend the Agricultural Stabilization Act. First, I would like to define
May 17, 1985

the situation surrounding this Bill, the situation on the farm front across Canada.
The Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) and the Hon. Member from Newfoundland began to define the kind of crisis situation which faces our farmers. This is probably the basic reason this Bill is before us, and why it was put before the previous Government about two years ago. It is the reason we so often stand in this House to speak about the problems of the farmers.
When the economic statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) was laced before this House last fall it was quite a blow to many farmers who suddenly realized that the bureaucracy, and many Hon. Members of the House of Commons, had no real insight into the problems of farming and agriculture. The economic statement of the Minister of Finance indicated a type of farm structure and return from farming which put the farmers in a category above most ordinary citizens. Exactly the opposite is true. A large portion of farmers, even the ones who appear to be well off, are living off their equity. Their equity is going down and their investment is going up. If one made that kind of investment in any other business in Canada, one would expect approximately 10 per cent or 12 per cent return on the investment. It is many years since the farmer received any return on his investment. That is the situation with which we are faced as this Bill is brought forward.
The Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville mentioned farm bankruptcies, as did the Hon. Member from Newfoundland. In 1979 there were 125 bankruptcies. In 1984 there were 551 bankruptcies. In the first three months of 1985, there have already been 152 bankruptcies. Those bankruptices are just the tip of the iceberg, Mr. Speaker, because most farmers recognize that they are going under and sell a piece of land in order to keep going for one more year, or they sell off half their herd. They decide they are not going to make it so they get out before they go bankrupt. They voluntarily leave farming. So the real problem is that farmers are leaving farming. Farms are being consolidated and a way of life of which we have been so proud is beginning to change. That change is not for the better because the person who takes over, although he may farm on a larger scale, faces exactly the same problems of too much debt and not enough return. Therefore, any kind of approach which would make survival of the farm community more certain is worthwhile taking.
1 am pleased that the Government has brought forward this Bill. I hope that in the process of coming to some kind of acceptable Bill in the end, the Liberals and the Conservatives do not close the door, because this Bill is almost identical to the previous Bill. I hope they do not close ranks behind the Bill and exclude the possibility of making it worthwhile, because right now it is not a worthwhile Bill.
The farmers are not making enough return on their investment to survive. By suggesting that perhaps if we give them a little more for their commodity in the years in which they have a commodity to sell they possibly might survive is too much of a gamble. We must have something in place which is more
Agricultural Stabilization Act
secure than the idea that we can stabilize farm commodities, that the farmer will get 90 per cent of what he received for the last five years. As the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville suggested, if the market price continues to go down, we are stabilizing a lower price each year, and if the cost of operations continue to go up, the spread between the income of the farm and the cost of farming becomes closer, until finally the positions are reversed. That is the situation which faces many beef farmers today.
In one township in my riding, 36 square miles, a few years ago there were something like 2,000 cattle. One would be hard pressed to find 500 cattle in that area now. This has happened over the last four years or five years when farmers, although they have hung on, have lost money. Instead of going bankrupt they have got rid of their cattle in the hopes they could make it on straight grain.
Statistics Canada shows that in 1975, the income from farming was $10 billion. In 1984, it was doubled at $20 billion. That seems as if we are doing very well, that we have twice as much income from farming. But that is the gross income. But over that same period of time we have increased the costs of operation from $6.6 billion to $16.6 billion. In 1975 some 65 per cent of the farmer's gross income went to cover expenses. That left 35 per cent for gross profits, although that is being a little simplistic. But in 1984 some 82 per cent of gross farm income went to cover depreciation and operating expenses.
Several Members have said that the farmer's net income in 1984 is the same as it was in 1974, and that is correct. But that does not take into account the change in the value of the dollar. In constant dollar terms, farm income in 1984 is $1.9 billion, compared with $3.8 billion in 1974. In other words, it has been halved over that period of time, and that cannot go on. Therefore, this Government and the provincial Governments across Canada must do something about it.
We could spend a lot of time looking at the need for this Bill, but what we should be looking at is something that will make it possible for farmers to survive. We need a system of stabilization insurance that deals with the farmer's income, not the price of his commodity.
If you ask a beef producer, he will tell you that it is costing him at least 25 per cent more to raise an animal than he is going to get back. This Bill, if we allow it to go through unchanged, will stabilize that 25 per cent loss and in fact make it possible for that loss to be increased as time goes by, because the stabilization is based on 90 per cent of the average price over the past five years. Although this stabilization plan is a step forward, because over a short period of time you might have a dramatic price drop and this plan would even out the bump, as time goes on, unless the market improves, it will not help the farmer. So why not look at the farmer's total income and then put in place something to make it possible for that farmer to survive under almost any circumstances, or at least in those years when his returns are low.

May 17, 1985
Agricultural Stabilization Act
A farmer faces not only market price problems, he faces bad weather, insect infestation and other problems. Therefore, farmers do not need just price stabilization. What good does it do if the price of grain is stabilized at $5 a bushel but the farmer has no grain to sell because it froze or the grasshoppers ate it? In the last two years we have had grasshopper problems in southeastern and southwestern Saskatchewan, and it looks like we are going to have another year of the same.
In approaching this Bill in committee we need to ask whether it does for farmers what is necessary. Does it put in place a survival plan so that in a bad year the farmer can survive, and in a good year he can make up what he lost in the bad year? As one farmer told me not too long ago, if he keeps this up for the next 10 years he will live but he will have nothing left, his equity will be zero. I think that is the situation faced by many farmers today. So this Bill is basically a step in the right direction, but it is so inadequate that we have to look at the basic problem and try to solve it in its entirety rather than piecemeal.
I could criticize small parts of the Bill, Mr. Speaker. For example, it does not establish one program, it establishes four programs. It is quite possible for the Government to carry on under this Bill in exactly the same way as before without any contribution, and perhaps farmers will accept that; no contribution and some payout under certain circumstances. It also allows the Government to make a deal with a province and not bring the producers into it at all. There has been considerable suggestion that the Bill is a tripartite approach, but it is not. It can be operated as a federal Government subsidy program alone, a provincial program alone, a federal-producer program, omitting the provincial Government, or a tripartite program, which has gotten the most publicity.
The farmers are looking to this Government for help. The Conservatives made a good start when they invaded Prince Albert during the election and made a lot of good promises about what they were going to do for farming, agriculture in general and transportation. The farmers look to them to fulfil their promises, but they also look to them to take a logical and worthwhile approach to agriculture generally. Although this Bill is almost exactly the same as the Whelan Bill of a year ago, it at least gives us an opportunity to air the problems faced by the agricultural community.
I am very glad that the Private Members' Bill on parity prices put before this House by the Hon. Member for York-ton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) is also being referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture so it can be discussed relative to this particular approach as well.
I think that some day in Canada we will have a stabilization insurance program for agriculture under which the farmer will be assured of receiving an adequate income when the grasshoppers get him or when the frost gets him, or when there is too much rain or not enough. That is what we need. This Bill eases the pain but farmers are still going down the drain. If this Government really wants to do something worthwhile for the farmers it will look at farming as a basic industry and recognize it as being essential, just as fisheries and forestry are
essential. We must decide what is necessary for them to survive, and then take certain steps in that direction.
Farmers do not want hand-outs. They want to be assured that in bad years caused by poor markets, insects, or frost, they can still make a living. That is the approach that should be taken. We are not short of ideas on how it could be done. Recently the Grain Production Committee of the Canada Grains Council presented a paper to a convention of municipal councils. It laid out a very effective-sounding income insurance plan for farmers. That idea should be studied, even though it probably has some faults. My Party and I and other Members in the House are not going to wed ourselves to one particular position. However, let us consider the idea of income insurance for farmers.
It would be ridiculous for the worker on the street to pay a large amount of money to ensure that his wages do not fluctuate, because that does not happen. However, it happens every year for farmers. Other workers pay for unemployment insurance in case they do not have a job next year. Therefore, the idea of insurance may be one which we should consider. Perhaps we should combine insurance with stabilization. In every case the basic approach should be the consideration of what is necessary for farming and farmers to survive.
This Bill is inadequate. It is almost identical to the original Whelan Bill. There is a great need to establish a comprehensive income insurance plan and this Bill does not accomplish that. Let us hope that when this Bill goes to committee we will take a global approach and allow the Committee on Agriculture to make amendments, or to rewrite the Bill in such a way as to take into consideration the needs of the industry, rather than just applying a band-aid to a number of the commodity areas.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great attention to the thoughtful speech of the Hon. Member. I would ask him for his comments on how he would resolve the apparent impasse which exists with some provinces that are unwilling to enter into an agreement to make this a national initiative with the support of all the provincial organizations affected.

Mr. Speaker, the Member has put his finger on one of the weaknesses of this Bill. There is such a variety of plans available, all of which are voluntary. If you do not volunteer for anything, you will not get anything. In the industry we have established a number of approaches for certain products. Each of the three western provinces with the responsibility to market grain agreed to give up that responsibility to the federal Government. The Canadian Wheat Board was established in 1926 and was legislated into existence in 1934. It is a central marketing system rather than managed production. This has proven that we can do that kind of thing. The dairy industry in every province has agreed to establish a dairy commission. This involves a bit of market management which certain commodity producers, such as the cattlemen in western Canada, do not want. However, it has been done with
May 17, 1985

eggs as well. There is the possibility for that kind of agreement if the structure which would allow it were in place.
There is a certain amount of insurance in the Dairy Commission and Egg Commission because the price received is based on production. Some people dislike that because it restricts their amount of production. That is being very shortsighted because if twice the amount of milk is produced the price would immediately go down and you would not make any more money in the end. To get the security you must give up something. If the Government put the structure in place I think we would get the necessary agreement across Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) started his remarks by saying that it is not a worthwhile Bill at present. The Bill would clarify and make more flexible the period on which the support price for any commodity would be based. I ask the Member whether that is not a worthwhile feature. Second, the Bill would allow for support periods to be shorter than a year, but not less than 90 days. Is that not worthwhile? Third, the Bill would include winter and spring wheat produced outside the designated wheat board area and a list of named commodities. Is that not worthwhile? The Bill would replace "sheep" in the list of named commodities with "lamb and wool". Is that not worthwhile? The Bill would provide a new framework for federal-provincial agreements. I ask the Hon. Member whether that is not a worthwhile concept? The Bill would provide for the appointment of staff of the Agricultural Stabilization Board under the Public Service Employment Act. Does the Member not feel that that is worthwhile?

Mr. Speaker, I have voted for and worked for stabilization at every level because it affects a particular individual at a particular time. This Bill affects drastic drops which can occur over a short period of time. However, because we are not solving the problem of agriculture in its entirety, perhaps it is just extending the agony. Maybe it is just allowing the industry to take a little longer to go broke. Maybe it will just take a little longer before we have the same situation as that which exists in Kansas. Soon, nearly 75 per cent of the farms in Kansas will be corporately owned. They will not necessarily be corporately farmed, but they will be corporately owned. That is happening in Canada.
The changes which the Member has suggested as worthwhile are the good features of the Bill. However, they are not solving the basic problem of agriculture, and neither is the Farm Credit Corporation or the capital gains changes which we are hoping the Government will introduce. All of those things are having some effect, but they are not solving the basic problem of agriculture.
During the next four years the Government should consider that basic problem because agriculture will suffer much more than it is today. We were much better off on the farm four years ago than we are today.

subtopic: THE CONSTITUTION ACTS, 1867 TO 1982 SENATE REFORM
THE CONSTITUTION ACTS, 1867 TO 1982 SENATE REFORM
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Constitution Acts, 1867 to 1982, should be amended in order to reform the Senate of Canada so that its membership is elected by the Canadian people and equal in representation of the provinces, thereby ensuring that the Senate of Canada would become effective legislative body.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I put this motion forward.

I would like to begin by stating some of the reasons I am propelled to introduce this motion. During the recent election campaign, as a political scientist, I thought that the issue of Senate reform was a dry and dusty one. I was astonished to discover that it has been one of the most lively issues among my constituents over the past year. In fact, at 44 public meetings held during the nomination campaign and the campaign itself the issue voluntarily came up at least once at each of those meetings. It is a pressing issue in western Canada.
I had occasion last Sunday to visit Peterborough, a beautiful city in central Canada. The occasion was the rededication of the monument to Captain Edward Templeton Brown who was a soldier with Bolton's Scouts and happened to have been killed at the Battle of Batoche. He was one of General Middleton's soldiers. I was called upon without notice to make some remarks since Captain Brown was my great uncle. I sought to convey something of a western perspective of what the Battle of Batoche means to western Canada. As tactfully as I could, in the presence of the Union Jack and the Red Coats, I strove to underline that the Riel phenomenon and Dumont's generalship really were a popular reaction in many ways to what was perceived as colonialization from elsewhere.
It is interesting to note from where the support for a Triple E Senate is beginning to come. While I am not sure if the

May 17, 1985
The Constitution Acts, 1867 to 1982
Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) has totally embraced the concept, he seems to be leaning in that direction. I suspect that many of our friends from the New Democratic Party, at least those who are westerners and perhaps others, are very sympathetic in their hearts and perhaps even in their minds. Of course, they are restrained by doctrine not to speak out on the issue.
Let me refer to some of the distinguished Canadians who have given their public support and financial support to the Triple E movement. They are the Hon. E. C. Manning, retired senator and former Premier of Alberta for some 25 years; Mr. Gordon Gibson, former Leader of the British Columbia Liberal Party; Mr. Jim Gray, Executive Vice President of Canadian Hunter Ltd; Mr. Ralph Hedlin, a distinguished energy policy consultant who lives in Ottawa; Mr. Horace Carver, former Attorney General of the Government of Prince Edward Island; and Mr. Ted Byfield, former publisher of the Alberta Report in Edmonton, Alberta. There is also our distinguished colleague, the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), who has served for 45 years in the legislatures of Canada, and Mr. Izzy Asper, Chairman of Canwest Capital Corp., in Winnipeg, Manitoba, a former Leader of the Opposition in the Liberal Party in that province. There is the distinguished Senator E. W. Barootes; Mr. Jack Gallagher; and Mr. Thomas P. d'Aquino, who is the President of the Business Council on National Issues which is based in Ottawa.
I would be remiss if I did not touch on some of the interesting developments in the direction of Senate reform over the past few years. The House will recall that in 1969, the then Government introduced a White Paper proposing a new Senate, with half of the members appointed by the provinces and the other half by the federal Goveinment. In 1972, the special Joint Committee of the Senate and the House on the Constitution recommended increasing the number of western senators and reducing the Senate's powers to a suspensive veto. In 1975, a constitutional amendment awarded one Senate seat to the Yukon Territory and the Northwest Territories, bringing the total membership to 104 Senators.
In 1978, Bill C-60 proposed replacing the Senate with a House of the Federation, with the provinces and the federal Government each appointing half the members based on por-tional representation. In 1979, the Supreme Court ruled that the proposals represented a constitutional amendment and would therefore require the approval of provincial legislatures as well as the federal Parliament.
In that same year of 1978, the Canada West Foundation recommended replacing the Senate with a House of the Provinces. British Columbia, the Ontario Advisory Committee on Confederation and the Canadian Bar Association also submitted reform proposals.
In 1979, the Pepin-Robarts Task Force on Canadian Unity proposed replacing the Senate with a provincially appointed Council of the Federation.
In 1980, the federal and provincial Ministers responsible for constitutional matters discussed a new Upper House involving the provinces, with no resolution. The report of the Standing
Senate Committee on Legal and Constitutional Affairs entitled "Certain Aspects of the Canadian Constitution", affirmed the need for a nominated but substantially reformed Senate.
The Quebec Liberal Party's Beige Paper entitled "A New Canadian Federation" proposed replacing the Senate with a federal council composed of provincial government delegates. In 1981 the well respected Canada West Foundation supported direct election of senators based on single province-wide constituencies.
In 1982, the Constitution Act provided for a six-month suspensive veto for the Senate in respect to constitutional amendments. Alberta recommended provincial appointment of Senators. The Senate debated the election of Senators by the people.
In 1983, a special joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on Senate reform started its work in April of that year. The Business Council on National Issues supported direct election of senators.
In 1984, the final report of the Special Joint Committee on Senate Reform was tabled in January.
This year, the Alberta Select Committee reported, and in May of this year the Hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) introduced his resolution.
Let me give credit to a distinguished former Member of the House who has done considerable research on the question of Senate reform. He is Mr. Bill Yurko, the former Member for Edmonton East. Mr. Yurko pointed out in a paper prepared three years ago, which was called "Toward a Renewed Senate Structure under the New Constitution", that a new Senate would require legitimacy, accountability, independence and stability. Mr. Yurko said that the issue of legitimacy is primarily a question of the Senate's legitimate position in the political process. He went on to say that probably nothing has undercut the Senate's position more than the system of Prime Ministerial appointments.
To be legitimate, any system which replaces the current regime must be structured to permit the Senate to perform its two most important functions in a balanced manner. The selection committee must be based in the regions or provinces to legitimize the regional representation function. It must allow for the selection of experienced politicians and other public figures to legitimize the legislative review or "sober second thought" functions. In relation to the Lower House, the second Chamber must also be a secondary chamber in every way. The House of Commons must remain supreme.
The second principle is that of accountability. Appointments for life steadily eroded the Senate's legitimacy. The central point at issue here is the question of accountability. The need to create a democratically accountable Upper House was not a high priority with the delegates to the Quebec conference. However, over the years, the lack of accountability has supplied abolitionists with ample ammunitions with which to wage their war against the Upper House.
May 17, 1985

The third principle is that of independence. To be effective a reformed plan must scrupulously uphold the independence of the Upper House. While expecting perfect and absolute independence from any legislative body may be unrealistic, the structural features of a reformed Senate should strive toward the ideal.
The final principle of a reformed Senate is that of stability. This is more or less separate from the question of which selection procedure would be preferable, since either election or modified appointment procedure could be tailored to provide stability. Whatever selection procedure is decided upon, Senators must have a longer term than Members of Parliament to allow them to develop the experience and expertise they require for legislative review and regional representation.
Let us go to the question of what the public seems to be saying on this issue of Senate reform. I go to two distinguished newspapers, two editorials published hard on the heels of the release of the joint committee report in early 1984.
The first is the Calgary Herald which reported:
The latest report on Senate reform hits one target dead on but is completely off the mark in proposing regional representation by population that leaves eight provinces still with no more than second-class status-
Three weeks before the walk in the blizzard, on February 3, 1984, in The Edmonton Journal we find this article:
An elected Senate, based on regional interests with significant power, would go part of the way toward making Ottawa everybody's national capital-not just those who voted for the party in power. Reform of the House of Commons itself would go the rest of the way ... Without Senate reform, Canada risks a permanent crisis of national unity and inferior policy-making-provincial premiers will continue to serve as the effective opposition to the federal party in power-The highest road for Prime Minister Trudeau's exit from politics would be full Parliamentary approval of this report-throwing the political and moral initiative to the premiers and the people of the provinces.
Obviously the challenge was not met at that time.
Why should this resolution be brought before the House at this time? We have before us now a resolution from the Minister of Justice to amend the Constitution in such a way as to limit the amount of time the Senate could delay money bills. We are told that agreement has been secured from eight of the Provinces to support this resolution-
