speechtext: Name them.

subtopic: THE CONSTITUTION ACTS, 1867 TO 1982 SENATE REFORM
speechtext:
-to support this resolution and that a constitutional conference will be held no later than 1987 to discuss long-term meaningful Senate reform. Whether those provincial commitments will hold is, I hear, now being questioned. Whether the Senate as it is now constituted will support the resolution remains to be seen. However, whether or not the resolution succeeds, the conference, we understand, will take place.
This is the time to coalesce the various proposals advanced for reform. Between now and 1987, let us develop in this place, in the other House and in public forums across the land a consensus for meaningful and enduring improvement.
The Constitution Acts, 1867 to 1982
The joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons basically made these recommendations: Senators be elected for non-renewable nine year terms by plurality vote in single member constituencies, in triennial elections separate from Commons elections, and that the Senate have a suspensive veto of 120 sitting days over most Bills; the representation of the less populous provinces and of the Territories would be increased, bringing the number of seats in the Senate to 144; legislation of linguistic significance would require a double majority vote; and the constituencies themselves would have a logic as to mutual interset.
I would like to take one moment now to outline the proposals of the Alberta Legislative Committee on Senate Reform, which has met with fairly wide approval, including very recently that of the distinguished Liberal Senator Dean Gigantes.
I will now outline the recommendations in summary, Mr. Speaker. First, that the Senate should continue to act as a body of sober second thought. Another original purpose of the Senate, that is to represent property owners, should be abandoned immediately. Third, the Senate should not be a forum for intergovernmental negotiations. It is recommended, vis-avis membership, that the tenure of current Senators should be terminated through an equitable severance process. Second, that the determination of tenure should be accomplished as quickly as possible to facilitate an immediate move to the new system.
On the method of selection and basis of representation of new Senators, it is recommended that the Senate should consist of 64 Senators, six representing each province and two representing each Territory. Senators should be elected on a first-past-the post basis, a system now in use in federal and provincial elections. Senators should represent constituencies whose boundaries are identical to provincial boundaries. Senators should be elected for the life of two provincial legislatures. In each province, three Senators should be elected during each provincial election with each voter being able to vote for three candidates. The qualifications should be the same as those for Members of Parliament. Upon winning an election, Senators should be required to resign from any provincial or civic elected office they hold.
With reference to the powers of the Senate, it is recommended that the Senate should have the power to initiate any legislation except a money or a taxation Bill. Notwithstanding that point, the Senate should have the power to initiate supply resolutions relating to the Senate's own operational Budget. The Senate should have the power to amend any Bill after which the House of Commons would consider the amendment. The Senate should have the power to veto any Bill except a supply Bill. The Senate should retain the existing 180 days suspensive veto over constitutional issues. The House should have the power to over-ride a Senate veto on money or taxation Bills by a simple majority, The Senate should vote on a money or taxation Bill within 90 days and on other Bills within 180 days after it is sent by the House of Commons. All changes affecting the French and English languages in Canada

May 17, 1985
The Constitution Acts, 1867 to 1982 should be subject to a double majority veto, that is a majority of all Senators combined with a majority of French speaking Senators or English speaking Senators, depending on the issue. This, Mr. Speaker, is from the legislature of Alberta. Finally, non military treaties should be subject to ratification by the Senate, to which I would suggest we add the appointment of deputy ministers, assistant deputy ministers, heads of Crown agencies, and commissions.
Current polls seem to indicate that Canadians have little faith in the Senate, primarily because of its method of appointment. In my part of the country, as well as I think in others, there is a feeling that regardless of the popularity or sensitivity of this Government, fundamental changes to Confederation are required in order to ensure that the Western and Atlantic provinces, in particular, are adequately represented in the federal decision-making process. In the west it is a particularly crucial issue. I will quote from my distinguished colleague, the Flon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) who said before the last election that western Canadians must feel that Parliament is protecting their legitimate interests; it is a very serious matter should that faith be lost. He went on to say that western Canadians do not feel that we Opposition Members are that effective; therefore, the emphasis is on the provincial premiers to defend them and that distorts the whole federal-provincial relationship. He went on to say that:
People now must vote for provincial premiers based on their effectiveness in opposing the government in Ottawa, whereas they want to be able to rely on Parliament itself-opposition Members, government Members and the Senate- for that.
Finally, there are oxen to be gored and hurdles to be overcome. The oxen to be gored include, of course, the powers of this very House, the powers of the Cabinet, the Prime Minister's office and perhaps most significantly the power-brokers themselves, the provincial premiers. But, Mr. Speaker, an effective elected Senate, equal in representation province to province, will bring to Canada the harmony and civility which have too often eluded us. This is not just something to please the west, though it would without doubt. It is not just a redress of the blows of history, economics and demography, dealt to the Atlantic Provinces. Nor is it a gimmick to bring Quebec warmly and securely back into the bosom of Confederation. It is an evolution whose time has come, for Ontario no less than for all of Canada.
Throughout the country, audiences of up to 3,000 people have cheered the concept of a Triple E Senate. It is the positive enduring alternative to confrontation. What better time to bring it to reality than as a crowning achievement of this new age of harmony and consultations.

subtopic: THE CONSTITUTION ACTS, 1867 TO 1982 SENATE REFORM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate this afternoon. I have read the motion of the Hon. Member. Some parts of it worry me personally, and I would like to speak to them.
I find it passing strange that over the last three or four months Conservative Members have introduced several motions, contradicting each other of course, on Senate reform.
One Member said that we should have an elected Senate, that if we could not have one, we should abolish the place. Another Member rose and said that the Senate was a great place. Now an Hon. Member today wants to considerably reapportion Senate representation and retain it as a useful and effective body.

subtopic: THE CONSTITUTION ACTS, 1867 TO 1982 SENATE REFORM
speechtext: It is a sign of a healthy Party.

subtopic: THE CONSTITUTION ACTS, 1867 TO 1982 SENATE REFORM
speechtext:
I suppose the Hon. Member for Nanaimo-Alberni (Mr. Schellenberg) has a good point. He says that it is a sign of a healthy Party that its Members can at least say something during Private Members' Hour. I am glad that there is at least one time of the day when Tories are permitted to do that. Hopefully they will muster up enough courage to do the same when we are considering legislation, but we will not hold our breath. Be that as it may, I should like to return to the debate at hand.
The sudden interest in the Senate on the part of the Conservatives has arisen because one day the Senate refused to give automatic consent to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to borrow funds for a year for which he had not tabled estimates. Of course the Minister of Finance should have never requested those funds, to start with. That day the Senate was guilty of doing its job. It is unusual that whenever the Senate is not doing its job, Conservatives talk about reforming the place. Whenever the Senate does its job, suddenly they talk about abolishing it. I find that passing strange. However, in my view we have to retain, protect and enhance our parliamentary institutions. This means that they should be reformed.
In the past, members of the New Democratic Party have always said that the Senate had to be abolished. Undoubtedly that is part of their doctrine. One fine day many, many years ago, a socialist awoke in the morning after dreaming that the Senate should be abolished, and thereafter it formed part of the Party doctrine. Of course it will hot happen and should not happen.
Most federal states have bicameral legislatures. The reason for this is to ensure that regional interests are represented and to overview legislation. This as well is the reason for having and retaining our Senate of Canada. The difficulty I have with the NDP proposition of abolishing the Senate will become evident if I remind the House that in 1979 the Government of the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) had very few Quebec Members. As a matter of fact, there were only two, one of whom was appointed to Cabinet. That created a very difficult situation in that one of the two founding peoples of our country was not represented in Cabinet. Therefore it was necessary at that time to call upon parliamentarians who did not sit in the House of Commons to join the Cabinet. Of course there was only one place with federal parliamentarians in our system of Government other than the House of Commons and that was the Senate. Therefore a number of people from existing Senate ranks were appointed to the Cabinet of the then Prime Minister. Thus there was regional representation in Cabinet provided by some other means than the House of Commons. It was made necessary because there was not a
May 17, 1985

sufficient number of Members elected not only from that province but from that linguistic group or founding nation. As I said previously, because there was not that representation the then Prime Minister rightly chose to appoint some Senators to Cabinet.
Another difficulty I have with the NDP proposition is that all of us in the House, collectively and individually, although Members on the government side do not usually complain about it as much as opposition Members, are somewhat at odds with the fact that there is an ever-increasing concentration of power in Cabinet and not enough in parliamentarians generally. If we abolish one of our Houses of Parliament, obviously it would only lead to a further concentration of power within Cabinet. After all, we cannot enhance Parliament by destroying half of it.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) presented a motion to the House to make the Senate into a reading room. Of course I have some difficulty with that proposition because the Minister is effectively trying to abolish one of our parliamentary institutions, nothing else. There is only one way to deal with reform of the Senate and that is through comprehensive reform. We cannot arbitrarily take away one of the most important powers of one of our Houses of Parliament, and call it reform, because one day the Minister of Finance did not get his way. There has to be more to reform. That is not comprehensive reform. That is not adequate. Obviously the scheme of the Minister of Justice will get nowhere. I do not think he has the consent of eight provinces. I challenge the Hon. Member to name those eight provinces. It will be interesting for all of us to check to see whether there is agreement on the part of eight Premiers on reducing the Senate to a reading room, as the Hon. Member claimed.
During his remarks today the Hon. Member suggested that we should give the same number of Senate seats to each province. If we look back at the history of our country and the reasons for having the Senate, we see that one of its functions was to provide a sober second thought. Perhaps that can be accomplished by having any number of Members from any part of the country. After all, a function of the Senate is to review legislation and the regional aspect is somewhat less significant in that regard, although it is still a concern. Of course another one of its functions is to provide individual provincial representation in Parliament. As I said a while ago, that manifested itself in the case of the 1979 Progressive Conservative Government which lacked a fundamental component of representation.
Another difficulty which I see-and I think the Hon. Member forgot it in his proposal today-is that in the origin of the Senate it had another function, to represent not only the regions but the two founding nation principle of our country. When Canada east and Canada west joined in the Act of Union of 1840 they were given equal or proportionate representation.

subtopic: THE CONSTITUTION ACTS, 1867 TO 1982 SENATE REFORM
speechtext:
Upper Canada?
The Constitution Acts, 1867 to 1982

subtopic: THE CONSTITUTION ACTS, 1867 TO 1982 SENATE REFORM
speechtext:
No, not Upper Canada; it was after Upper Canada. Upper Canada was 1791 to 1840, but in the Act of Union of 1840 Canada east and Canada west were joined. At that particular time there was identical representation in both Houses, notwithstanding the fact that Canada east had a larger population than Canada west. Canada west, Ontario, was given a much larger number of seats. It was known at that time that the population of Canada west would increase. Canada east accepted an equal representation because there was a two founding nation principle that was important to preserve. Those statistics have turned around and numerically in terms of Anglophones and Francophones there is now a far greater number of Anglophones in this country.
The same principle was very important in the deliberations in the 1860s in the Constitutional Conference where Canada east and Canada west, formerly called Upper Canada and Lower Canada, wanted a parliamentary structure in which there would be equal representation in at least one of the Houses of Parliament of those two areas. The Maritime provinces, which were then about to join Canada, wanted at least as much power together as one of the two larger provinces. The reluctance they had as smaller Maritime provinces was based on their fear that the difficulty that existed between Canada east and Canada west would put them in the middle of the problem. They wanted to ensure that collectively the Maritime provinces had at least as much power in one of the Houses of Parliament as Canada east and Canada west. Those are some of the origins.
When the western Canadian provinces joined Confederation under various parliamentary Acts of 1870, 1905 and so forth, they were given a number of Senate seats, again proportional to one of the other regions that existed. This created a situation whereby French Canada, Quebec, had and still has approximately one-quarter of the Senate seats in this country. Perhaps that is somewhat more than their fair share in terms of percentages. There is an element outside the percentages which cannot be measured. That principle has to be measured differently, the principle of the two founding nations. It is important to remember that.
I hope there is not one Member in this House, particularly from Quebec, who would want to restructure our parliamentary institution to remove some of those special powers and privileges that are necessary to ensure not only that each province is represented, but that there is a special place in confederation for French Canada. By giving one-tenth of the representation in the Senate to French Canada, and giving an equal number of seats to all provinces, one-tenth or one-eleventh, depending on how many seats there are for the Territories-giving roughly one-tenth of the representation of the Senate to the Province of Quebec is unacceptable. I hope that Members will reconsider any such proposal, however well-intentioned it might be.
I think the Hon. Member's remarks were very positive with regard to enhancing the parliamentary institution, and I com-

May 17, 1985
The Constitution Acts, 1867 to 1982 mend him for that, but the formula he suggested is not correct. I am sure that all who are concerned about the two founding nation principle of this country will agree that there has to be a special element in the parliamentary structure to protect that principle. We all know of the special provisions that are there for Quebec. We know of the guaranteed minimum number of seats for that province. Only one province in Canada has a guaranteed minimum number of seats in the House of Commons. All other provinces cannot have less seats in the House than they have in the Senate.
Quebec has another tier of guarantee which is very important, and rightfully so. It has to be there. I say this as a Member who does not represent that province. I am a Franco-Ontarian who represents a linguistic group that is similar and, although I am from outside the province, I am very interested in that topic. It is very important in my mind, as it should be in the minds of all parliamentarians.
Quebec has a different method of designating Senate areas, ridings or electoral districts. Senators represent their provinces. That is true in all provinces except Quebec. In Quebec, Senators are each assigned an electoral district which is similar, if not identical, to the 24 seigneuries in the Province of Quebec. There is a special significance there for the Province of Quebec, and it is important to remember all these things.
How do we reform the Senate? In my view, we should have an elected Senate. I fully concur with that proposition. It is an ideal time to consider that seriously. I believe all Members of this House should advocate that. As elected parliamentarians and supporters of elected democratic institutions I am sure all Members want our parliamentary institutions to reflect that principle. However, we should not forget that destroying, dismantling or doing something in a way which is not well thought out will not necessarily enhance our Senate. We must proceed with caution and real reform, and do it all at once. It should be a comprehensive package, not one that addresses just one small part of the issue.
In order to reflect the principle that our Senate must represent provincial interests, I believe that Senators should be elected at provincial elections. While that may be a somewhat unusual way of proceeding, what better occasion is there to assess the provincial mood of an area than during the provincial election campaign? Why not elect one-half of the Senators at every provincial election, assuming that we had the same number of seats in the Senate that we have now in each province? I recognize that there has to be reform there. However, for the purpose of debate, let's assume that we have the same number of seats that we have in each province. The greatest number of Senators that could be changed at any one time would be 12. Ontario and Quebec each have 24 Senate seats. With only one-half elected in every provincial election, a maximum of 12 would change at any one time, if all Senators were defeated within that province, which is somewhat unlikely. There would be insured continuity.
Some Members may wonder how we could ensure that those Senators elected have at least some sort of federal point of view. If Senators were elected with very separatist tendencies,
for example, there could be some difficulty having that institution function. In order to present candidates for the Senate a Party should have a minimum number of seats in the House of Commons. There would then be a process which would marry the principle of federalism with the thoughts of electors in a provincial election campaign. In so doing, we would have a provincial perspective, federal perspective and continuity, because only a small number would be elected at any one time.
That theory has to be further developed. There needs to be a full airing of that view in order to ensure that the system would best represent our country. I recognize there has to be a way of looking at the proportion of Senators in each province. I agree with that. However, in so doing, we must keep in full view the fact that there must be a very special place for the Province of Quebec; we must retain that important component in the system.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to oppose this Bill as both previous speakers had suggested someone from my Party would. I have listened to the interesting lectures that have been given. However, I do not detect a clear enough thrust in either the remarks of the Hon. Member for Edmonton South (Mr. Edwards) or those of the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) to warrant a careful study of what they said. In fact, for a while, I thought the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell was debating a different motion entirely. He seemed to have imagined that the subject for debate was a resolution by the NDP for abolition of the Senate. However, toward the end of his remarks, he did return to the subject at hand.
I found the historical comments made by the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell regarding the rationale for the Senate from the past century and perhaps the early part of this century to be very interesting and informative. The mover of the motion gave us a rapid-fire survey of the more recent history of discussion regarding the Senate. I believe his object was to prove that Senate reform is an idea whose time has come because enough people have talked about it. It is no doubt true that a number of people have talked about it. However, at all-candidates meetings and other public meetings that have been held in the riding of Spadina, not only when I ran for office but at the time of previous elections when I did not run for office, this question seemed to come up very rarely. It may be that certain candidates, simply by their own expressions of interest, evoke more discussion around that subject than do other candidates.
Both Hon. Members mentioned a variety of schemes. Although the Triple E proposal made by the mover of the motion does state some broad principles, he developed it with so many alternatives from so many groups that it is difficult to see exactly how he would focus. Likewise, the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, in using up his last two or three minutes, proposed a whole new scheme as an alternative. He made very little development of the practical effect of the scheme.
May 17, 1985

The difficulty with both presentations is that the Hon. Members made an assumption which, in a doctrinaire way, they simply repeat without really defending. They made the assumption that we need a Senate. The Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell did make some attempt at defending the Senate, but he defended it largely in terms of the very early years of Canada's history, the years when different parts of the British Empire were being incorporated into Canada and there were growing pains. He picked out some instances of the existence of the Senate being important for the defence of either of the two founding nations of this country. However, I think it is a mistake to make an automatic assumption that because we had a Senate before, we must have it forever. Perhaps it is a venerable old piece of the furniture, but the question is whether or not it serves a function and, if so, whether that function is predominantly useful or harmful.
I think it is not at all clear that in balance, the function of the Senate is useful. As it exists at present, I doubt that it seriously defends the unity of Canada. I have not noticed that the things that tend to tear Canada apart are curbed by the Senate. It seems rather that the Senate at times intensifies the things that tear Canada apart. An example of this is its action a couple of years ago on banking legislation. Very frequently the effect of its action on banking legislation is to strengthen the grip of a tiny minority of powerful Canadians on the Canadian economy. Legislation that goes to the Senate from this House with the object of curbing the power of the banks tends to come back from the Senate with the object of increasing the power of the banks. That does not promote unity in this country. It may appear to do so by momentarily drawing attention away from rivalries between east and west, French and English, Maritimes and centre and North and South, but in fact it intensifies still greater rivalry or polarity.
Last year there was an example of action by the Senate which did not directly intensify a division, but was quite ineffectual for the public good. This happened when the previous Government put forward an outrageous piece of legislation designed to implement the security service of Canada. After the legislation was tramped on by Attorneys General across the country and by all sorts of public institutions, the Government referred it to the Senate. I think that this was meant to take the heat off the Government. The Senate sat on the matter for a few months and then brought the legislation back with some cosmetic changes. The Government felt that that was fine, it was a reformed Bill and it would now be passed. The Government did pass it. The Conservative Party which was then the Official Opposition supported the Bill in the end and throughout committee stage.
I was rather amused when I recently received a fund raising letter signed by Dalton Camp. He is asking for money for the civil liberties associations; one of the reasons he is doing so is that we have this dreadful legislation. I do not know where Dalton Camp was last year when the Party he helps to lead as one of the back-room boys was promoting that Bill in support of the Liberal Government. He is now trying to raise money for civil liberties associations and is saying that it was a bad
The Constitution Acts, 1867 to 1982
Bill. I do not remember the Senate being a house of sober second thought regarding that very important and very dangerous Bill that was passed by the Senate and by the House.
I do not see that the Senate performs a useful function. Granted if we are to have a Senate, it should be an elected one.
I do agree with the two previous speakers on that matter. An elected Senate would have to be less harmful than an appointed Senate. The question of whether or not it should have equal representation from all provinces, I think, tends to be irrelevant or ambiguous. Equal representation suggests that fundamental conflicts in the country that need to be balanced are conflicts between people in areas which are marked by some provincial boundary. Just because a certain line goes from north to south between Manitoba and Saskatchewan does not mean that the people in Saskatchewan have different interests from the people in Manitoba and must therefore have balanced representation in Parliament.
I grew up in Manitoba and I understand that there are tensions, but I find as decades go by they are less and less based simply on regional conflicts because the regions are changing. For example, the economic boom in the western provinces, particularly in Alberta and British Columbia, has considerably altered the balance of power within Canada. The regional considerations which may have seemed very strong when we had only Upper and Lower Canada, or Canada east and Canada west, or the Maritime Provinces plus Quebec and Ontario, not having yet incorporated Manitoba and points west, are now an important part of our history, but not necessarily part of our present needs. I do not remember the Senate doing anything serious to mediate the dispute with respect to the price of oil within Canada and the slogan of the western Premier, Mr. Lougheed, "Let those eastern bastards freeze".

May 17, 1985
The Constitution Acts, 1867 to 1982

subtopic: THE CONSTITUTION ACTS, 1867 TO 1982 SENATE REFORM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the debate during Private Members' Hour on Senate reform. I took particular interest in the comments of the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) who very often stands in the House of Commons to speak on many issues, and sometimes knows something about those issues. However, his exact comments, as I recall them, were that he was concerned about a special influence which certain provinces should retain in the Canadian Senate much the way they are in the House of Commons. I can understand his fear. I can understand, perhaps, the central Canadian's xenophobia of western Canadians rushing in here with all kinds of brilliant ideas. I can understand those comments and feelings because as a western Canadian I know that we have been in the wilderness for many, many years. The previous administration had only one elected representative in the Canadian Cabinet.
I believe that perhaps it is time for Senate reform which would allow us to have a little more influence in the Government of Canada. What the Hon. Member's comments basically stressed is that there is no need for reform, that we should have the private arrangements which were there before. I entirely disagree with that suggestion.
With respect to the comments of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Edmonton South (Mr. Edwards), I am in almost total agreement with him on many of the things he said. Perhaps it is because he and I shared those years in the wilderness. I find myself in basic agreement with the thrust of his comments, but I certainly disagree with the timing of which he speaks. My colleague knows the approach of our Government in proposing the constitutional resolution, now on the Order Paper, that deals with the absolute veto of the present Senate. The Hon. Member for Edmonton South is aware that this is merely an interim measure, with a constitutional conference scheduled before December, 1987 to discuss the issue of Senate reform in greater detail. The Hon. Member also knows that the consent of seven provinces with 50 per cent of the population of Canada is required in order to enact the changes he is suggesting.
We have all heard the expression, "If it ain't broke, fix it". I believe most Hon. Members in this chamber would agree that the Senate is not working as well as it could and perhaps it is time to fix it.
Let us take a look at this august body, the much maligned Canadian Senate. One journalist called it "The only wax museum in history where the figures actually breath". Vancouver humourist, Eric Nicol, said, "There are two kinds of people in Canada. There's the quick and there's the Senate". Columnist, Allan Fotheringham called it, "A body that bores the socks off most Canadians". Well, some of Mr. Fothering-ham's recent columns may also fall into that category, but we will not get into that.
Even the Right Hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) does not know what to make of the other place. As a 20-year-old student at the University of British Columbia he wrote in his bachelor of arts thesis in 1949, "If the Government summons men of experience and ability to the red chamber, and provides the upper House with enough work to do, there is no reason to doubt that the Senate will continue to manifest its present efficiency". But in 1961, the Right Hon. Gentleman seemed to have a change of heart. While practising law in Montreal he wrote an article lambasting the Senate as a haven of retired politicians and party bagmen. He said, "The waste of talent in recent administrations has made that chamber a functionalist oddity". There seems to be a lot of confusion all around, but I do submit that the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition was perhaps right the second time around.
Every so-called civilized country has a second chamber as some sort of a check on the first chamber. But I believe an appointed legislature, supported by public funds, has no place in a democratic society. That is my opinion. It is one man's opinion. What do the 24 million other Canadians think about reform of the Canadian Senate? I think we should take the time to find out, with debates such as this in the House of Commons, a constitutional conference with our premiers, and continued discussion with our constituents.
Like a bit player in the theatre, the other place since Confederation has stayed in the background. The audience is aware of its presence but the focus, as in any performance, remains on the leading players in the House of Commons. However, the bit player in our national drama has recently knocked over a prop and now stands exposed in the spotlight. Do we fire the bit player for his folly, or do we attempt to improve his performance? If we are going to improve his performance, how exactly do we do it? Some have suggested a ten-year term with elections every five years for half of that august body. Others have suggested nine-year terms with elections for a third of the members every three years. And I heard a couple of other suggestions from my colleague, the Hon. Member for Edmonton South this afternoon.
We do know that reform requires consent of seven of the provinces for major changes. Abolition is a little more difficult and requires the support of all ten provinces as it affects the amending formula under the Constitution. When the Fathers of Confederation scripted this great drama about which we have been speaking, they provided for a balance between the provincial legislatures and the federal Parliament. This provision, of course, was the "other place", which would be formed on a regional basis; 24 members from the west, 24 members from Quebec, 24 members from Ontario and 24 members from the Maritimes. The flaw in this scenario is that of the three bodies, the provincial legislatures, the House of Commons and the Senate; it is the other place which is the only one not made accountable to the people through elections.
Should the Liberals and their allies ever regain centre stage, it could well result in the electors of my great province of British Columbia being once again relegated to the cheap seats. On the other hand, as my colleague the Hon. Member for Edmonton South might agree, with a regionally elected Senate with appropriate muscle Alberta would not have to accept the crippling effects of the national energy policy, as it did in previous years.
May 17, 1985

Total abolishment would doom the regions to certain further abuse from future Governments. Total abolishment would also involve asking that dottering bit player to fall on his own sword which has, until recently, remained unsheathed. But more than that, Mr. Speaker, total abolishment would remove the possibility of a responsible second chamber with equal elected provincial representation. So I think my colleague the Hon. Member for Edmonton South and I are paddling the same canoe on this issue. We only differ on when we should arrive at the rapids.
I will conclude my comments, Mr. Speaker, by saying that a few years ago I recall an Opposition Member of Parliament,
The Constitution Acts, 1867 to 1982
probably one of those wise Conservatives our nation has come to know and love, saying that, "While Pierre Elliot Trudeau fiddled with the Constitution, the fire went out of the Canadian economy". Those fires are only now being rekindled. Employment initiatives, not Senate reform, are of paramount importance to the citizens of Canada.
